<document>
# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
I've read it. Here's my summary, to check I have the same thing:

**What it reports:** A registered 24-month follow-up of Varden plus 14 Halden organisations with record-based output. It sets out to settle three questions: does the gain persist, does the meetings finding survive a registered test, and do timesheets understate work.

- **Varden case-processing (randomised, administrative output):**
  - Output per hour: +9.8% on timesheets, +8.5% on system logs (CI 3.4 to 13.8).
  - Output per employee: −3.4% (CI −8.0 to +1.2).
  - Quality, sick days and resignations: effects held.
- **Mediation:** registered at month 11. Meetings explain 47% of the gain (CI 28–66), fatigue 18% (CI 2–34), and 35% is unexplained.
- **Unplanned observation:** two control offices cut meetings on their own initiative in month 15 and gained about 4% per hour.
- **Counter arm:** ended at month 12. Waits were 7.3 vs 4.0 minutes, and restoring service would have needed about 12% more staff.
- **Halden follow-up:** 3 of 14 organisations reverted (hospitality, retail, a marketing agency). The 11 that continued show +11.8% per actual hour, which the authors frame as an upper bound.
- **On the earlier papers:** "entirely an artifact" is not supported. The meta-analysis's four long-follow-up studies were all uncontrolled and used scheduled hours, so they can't speak to decay.

**Arithmetic check.** These figures check out:
- 0.966/0.88 = +9.8% and 0.966/0.89 = +8.5%.
- Halden: 96.8/86.6 = +11.8%.
- Mediation shares sum to 100%.
- Meetings difference-in-differences: (7.4 − 3.9) − (7.2 − 7.0) = 3.3 h.
- Counter staffing: restoring output needs 1/(0.83 × 1.067) ≈ 1.13, consistent with "about 12%" more staff. The 9% cost figure is plausible if non-staff costs are around a quarter of the total, but that should be stated.

**Overall.** This follow-up settles several questions that were open, and I should now treat them as settled rather than keep hedging. It also has two problems it doesn't see, one of which affects its own main estimate of decay.

## What this closes

- **The gain persists at 24 months, and it is not entirely an artifact.** The estimate uses randomisation, records, log-measured hours and two years of follow-up, which is everything Varga and Holm asked for. In this setting, the per-hour gain in discretionary work is about 8–10%. The 9-month version of this claim was supported but unsettled; I now consider it settled for this employer.
- **The no-decay claim is withdrawn.** All four long studies in the meta-analysis were uncontrolled and used scheduled hours. That confirms the design-mix concern I raised. The meta-analysis's statement that "novelty explanations can be set aside" should be withdrawn.
- **Counter work without extra staff doesn't hold up.** The waits now have a control comparison (7.3 vs 4.0), and the employer itself ended the arm. For this setting, the counter question is closed.
- **Timesheets understate hours only slightly.** Logs show about 1 point more work than timesheets. That question is closed too.
- **The baseline concern about meetings is resolved.** I worried the 9-month comparison of meeting time came from month six only, with no pre-period. The baseline data are now in, and they're balanced (7.4 vs 7.2). The 3.3-hour difference is now measured against baseline.

## What it doesn't see

**1. The control arm took up part of the treatment, which biases the decay estimate.** From month 15, two of the seven control offices adopted the hypothesised mechanism by cutting meetings, and gained about 4.1% per hour. That raises the control average by roughly 1.2 points (2/7 × 4.1) over months 16–24. This shrinks the measured treatment effect, so part of the like-for-like decline from 12.5% to 9.8% may be the control arm improving rather than the treated offices fading.

The report presents the audit as an interesting aside, without noticing that it contaminates its own decay estimate. What's needed:
- the 24-month estimate with those two offices excluded, or a version that accounts for their contamination;
- the treated offices' own trajectory over time;
- a formal test of the 9-to-24-month change.

The intervals overlap heavily (6.9–18.4 vs 4.6–15.2), so "declined" is a point-estimate statement, not a demonstrated decline.

**2. The summary overstates the decay.** It reports "12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months," which compares a timesheet figure with a log figure. The like-for-like comparison is 12.5% to 9.8%, a fall of about 22% rather than 32%, and section 5 itself uses that comparison ("about a quarter"). The summary should match it.

**3. Calling the meetings result "confirmed" overstates it.** The registration is real and it matters: it removes analytic flexibility. But three things limit how far it goes.

- **Not an independent replication.** The hypothesis was generated in these seven treated offices and retested on the same seven. It may also be retested on overlapping months, depending on whether the 24-month outcome covers months 13–24 or the whole period. The authors should state which.
- **Mediation assumptions.** The method assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediator and outcome, for example a manager who both cuts meetings and drives output. The limitations acknowledge this, but the summary doesn't.
- **Few clusters.** The interval rests on 7 vs 7 offices, so the small-cluster inference issue I raised for the 9-month report applies here too.

"Supports" is the accurate word. The meetings explanation has moved from weak to moderate evidence, which is a substantial step. But it is still one employer, one set of offices.

**4. Part of the meetings pathway may be built into the definitions.** The report needs to say exactly what "active log-in time" measures. If it is total working time, meetings included, then cutting hours spent in meetings that close no cases raises output per hour almost by accounting. That is the "remove low-value time" mechanism working as described, which is fine, but it means part of the 47% follows from the definitions rather than being discovered. If logs measure only time on cases, the arithmetic doesn't add up. Case time would then have fallen only about 3% (roughly 30.5 → 29.5 hours once meetings are netted out), and output per case-hour would be about flat, not +8.5%. Reporting output per total hour and output per case-hour separately would show how much of the gain is fewer unproductive hours and how much is faster work on cases.

**5. One reversion was in discretionary work.** "All with client-facing or coverage obligations" stretches a category to cover a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Marketing was a discretionary sector in the original pilot and in the meta-analysis's coding. With n = 1 it proves nothing, but the summary should say "two coverage-bound, one discretionary" rather than fit it to the story. The 14 of 23 response rate is another layer of selection, which the "upper bound" framing partly covers. The figures also have no control for productivity trends over two and a half years.

## Where this leaves the whole set

| Status | Finding |
|---|---|
| **Settled** | Pilot headlines were inflated by design and measurement. Per-worker output falls in coverage-bound work without extra staff, and in Varden the arm was abandoned. A real per-hour gain of about 8–10% persists for at least 24 months in discretionary public-sector work. It is not entirely an artifact, and the meta-analysis's "no decay" claim doesn't hold. |
| **Supported, not settled** | Some fading after the first year (size uncertain; see point 1). Meetings as the largest single pathway, with roughly half the gain (one trial, same offices). Output per worker slightly below control (CI includes zero). |
| **Open** | Whether reorganisation *without* cutting hours captures most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes it happen and stick. The control-office audit is suggestive, but no arm tested it. Also open: what happens beyond 24 months, and how this applies to private-sector, manufacturing and shift work. |

The first open question is now the most important for policy. The evidence suggests about half the gain comes from removing low-value time, which an employer might capture without cutting hours. A three-arm trial would test it directly: cut hours, reorganise only, or neither. The reorganise-only arm would need to be specified in advance, using the audit those two control offices improvised.

If useful, I can draft that three-arm design, or write the five-document synthesis as a short brief for a decision-maker.
